analysis.one_liner: Bans new hazardous and solid waste facilities within 5,000 feet of homes, schools, day cares, churches, and parks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died in a House subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a new rule into federal waste law: no hazardous waste treatment, storage, or disposal facility, and no solid waste facility of any kind, could be located within 5,000 feet of a home, day care, church, school, or park. It directed the Environmental Protection Agency to issue matching regulations within 90 days and applied the rule only to permits issued more than 120 days after enactment, so existing facilities could keep operating. The bill never moved beyond its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, learn, or worship near proposed waste facility sites, disproportionately in lower-income and minority neighborhoods, would gain a legal barrier keeping new hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities and other solid waste facilities at least 5,000 feet (about a mile) away from their homes, schools, day cares, churches, and parks. Existing communities near current sites would be protected from further expansion or new construction under the effective date, which applied only to permits issued after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near waste facility sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have barred owners and operators of hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities from locating them within 5,000 feet of residential property, day cares, churches, schools, or parks.

It would have required state solid waste plans to apply the same 5,000-foot restriction to all facilities for collecting, storing, recycling, or disposing of solid waste and recyclable materials, so landfills and transfer stations could not be sited next to neighborhoods either.
It would have directed the EPA to write implementing regulations within 90 days of enactment, rather than leaving the rule to slower standard-setting.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of hazardous and solid waste facilities would bear the cost: existing sites could not expand near protected properties, and new sites would have to be sited at least 5,000 feet from homes, schools, day cares, churches, and parks, which narrows available land and raises siting and disposal costs, some of which could be passed through to waste customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Waste disposal facility owners and operators

drawbacks.text: A 5,000-foot (roughly one mile) buffer applies nationwide regardless of local conditions and would rule out siting in many already-developed areas, which could concentrate new facilities in rural areas far from the waste they serve and raise transport and disposal costs.

The bill preempts local siting decisions by writing the distance rule directly into federal law and state plan requirements, taking the choice away from the state and local zoning processes that currently decide where facilities go.

The bill gives no funding or transition help for disposal capacity, so communities that lose nearby siting options could face higher waste fees while the underlying amount of waste generated stays the same.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents near proposed waste sites, the benefit is direct: a hard federal distance rule between hazardous and solid waste facilities and the places children and families spend their time, backed by EPA regulations on a 90-day deadline. The main costs fall on facility operators and, indirectly, on waste customers through higher disposal prices, and the one-size-fits-all 5,000-foot rule would have made siting harder in dense areas without any flexibility or funding for alternative capacity. On balance the bill traded a modest, industry-borne cost for a significant health and quality-of-life protection for the neighborhoods where these facilities are typically placed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a House committee and then a subcommittee and stayed there, never getting a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 26, 1997, with 15 Democratic cosponsors including John Lewis of Georgia, Bennie Thompson, and Danny Davis.
It was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced, and a week later to the Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote, never reached the House floor, and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Waste facility owners and operators are better off because the bill died: no federal buffer-zone rule was created, so siting near homes, schools, and parks remained governed by whatever state and local rules applied. Residents near proposed facility sites gained no new federal protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Waste facility operators facing no siting limits

for.name: Harold E. Ford Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a 5,000-foot buffer zone around homes, schools, day cares, churches, and parks.

for.name: 14 of 15 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original supporters.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee held no markup or vote and the bill never advanced past its subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote; all 15 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Commerce Committee took no action after referral.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal companies
industries.note: The bill would have barred locating hazardous waste treatment, storage, and disposal facilities within 5,000 feet of residential properties, day cares, churches, schools, and parks, restricting where new or expanded facilities could be sited. Because the bill died, the industry kept the existing siting rules, under which facilities have historically been placed disproportionately near minority and low-income neighborhoods.

industries.industry: Solid waste management and landfill operators
industries.note: The bill would have required state solid waste plans to impose the same 5,000-foot buffer on landfills, recycling, and other solid waste facilities, limiting siting options and raising disposal costs. Its defeat left the industry's siting flexibility intact.
